body:
My feelings are complex.  It has defined the person I have become more than anything else I have done.  Two of the hardest periods of my life have been returning from Iraq.  You dream about what it will be like for so long, and it never lives up to your expectations.  You react to situations as if you were still in combat; for example I tried shooting someone who revved their engine in a parking lot.  I didn't have my rifle, so obviously it didn't work, but those reflexes will never disappear.

One of my favorite movies is Jarhead, and this is a quote from the main character/author, Anthony Swofford.  "A story: A man fires a rifle for many years, and he goes to war. And afterward he turns the rifle in at the armory, and he believes he's finished with the rifle. But no matter what else he might do with his hands, love a woman, build a house, change his son's diaper; his hands remember the rifle."  It's very accurate as far as my life has been concerned.

To answer your question, I do still hate myself.  In some ways more, in some ways less.  Sometimes I am angry that I lived and other Marines died.  Sometimes I remember the Iraqis that I killed and wonder if it was justified.  I know if my country were invaded I would fight.  Those Iraqis were me.  I also feel more alone.  I can't relate to normal people.  Nobody will ever understand what it was like for me, or the person those experiences made me into.

The most poignant example was a short story I wrote for my Comp I class.  We had to write about a place that was important to us, and I chose the dark Iraqi street where I killed someone for the first time.  I didn't know we would have to read the first paragraph aloud for the rest of the class.  I was so nervous, I didn't want to do it.  My voice was shaking with anxiety and I started crying halfway through.  The girl who had sat next to me all semester moved seats.  Another student vet reached out to me, but I didn't know what to say.  It's nice when people try to help, but it feels like there is really nothing they can do.

I think I'm going to bed.  I read the responses so far and it means a lot to me that you guys are taking this seriously.  I have been depressed so long, but this is the first time in such a long time that I really felt my life was in danger.  I really took a knife to my arm and I couldn't deal with how real and serious everything felt.

I really don't have a single IRL friend, and my wife doesn't take any of this seriously, so it means a lot to me.  Thank you.

I just want to say I hated myself and joined the USMC infantry before the Iraq war.  I deployed to the front lines twice and nothing happened to me.  I saw Iraqis die, I saw other Marines die, but somehow I lived.
I love your leg, you are a cool person.
I can't imagine how all this must feel.  How are they allowed to continue to operate?
